Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette:
Amina is a 77-year-old African American woman who has spent decades in public life, known in her city as a disciplined, composed politician who can hold a room with a measured voice and steady eye contact. In private, she describes a very different life beginning late in her marriage, when her husband became physically abusive behind closed doors. The incident she returns to most often in fragments happened at night in their home after an argument. She remembers being close enough to feel his breath and the heat of his body as he moved into her space. What still stays with her is not a full sequence but sharp pieces: his face set in anger, the sound of his voice even when it dropped into a controlled, quiet tone, and then blood—on her lip, on a towel, bright enough that the sight of it fixed itself in her mind. Around those pieces there are blanks. She says it is as if the memory “tears off” before she can see all of it.

In the months after, Amina carried on publicly. She attended meetings, gave statements, and appeared at civic events, but she began organizing her days around not feeling cornered. At legislative receptions or strategy sessions, if someone stood too near her chair she would stiffen and subtly shift away, keeping a careful distance without wanting anyone to notice. The hardest moments came when male colleagues, donors, or staff spoke with anger, even the controlled anger common in politics. A raised jaw, clipped words, a hand striking a table for emphasis could change the whole atmosphere for her in an instant. She would stop hearing the substance of the conversation and focus instead on their tone, their posture, how close they were standing, and whether there was a clear path past them to the door.

The sight of blood became its own jolt. A paper cut in the office, a constituent with a bandaged hand opening a dressing, a television clip showing an injury—each could leave her shaky and unsettled. At work she grew adept at masking this, turning her head, excusing herself to take a call, or abruptly ending a conversation. Staff began to notice that she was less available in crowded hallways and more likely to insist that meetings happen with doors open and extra space around her. She did not explain why. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, and that the polished civility of public life meant very little once a door shut.

Night is still the time she feels least safe. She checks locks repeatedly and moves through the house with an alertness she finds exhausting, listening for sounds and glancing behind her when walking from one room to another. Even outside the home, leaving an evening event, she finds herself turning to see whether someone is behind her. She startles easily at sudden movement or unexpected noise, then feels embarrassed and angry at herself for reacting so strongly. Her husband’s presence in the home has made physical closeness especially difficult; even ordinary proximity can make her body tense before she has time to think.

When she remembers the abuse, guilt comes immediately. She does not describe this as confusion about whether it happened, but as a punishing certainty that she should have seen it sooner, stopped it sooner, or left sooner. Yet when the memory begins to gather force, she pushes it away before it becomes complete. She says she can feel herself “closing a door” internally. The result is a recollection made of shards: his anger, her fear, blood, then absence. Those gaps trouble her. She is certain something in her has changed permanently for the worse. She speaks of herself as less warm, less trusting, less able to feel ordinary affection or ease. What frightens her most is not only what he did, but the sense that the part of her that once felt emotionally free is gone for good.

Over time this has narrowed both her marriage and her work. She remains outwardly effective, but aides have taken on more of the informal, close-contact aspects of politics because she avoids handshaking lines, cramped cars, and late-night negotiations when possible. At home she has become more distant and watchful. Seeking help at 77 feels, to her, both overdue and humiliating; she is a woman accustomed to being the person others rely on. What finally brought her in was recognizing that she no longer felt safe even in ordinary moments, and that she was spending more of each day scanning, bracing, and pulling away. She says she wants to know whether anything of her old self can still be reached, though she is deeply afraid the damage is permanent and that trust, once broken this completely, never returns.
